title: Public Beliefs about Falsehoods in News
screen_reason: Two-wave comparative election panel survey in the United States, the United Kingdom and France (2017) that asks respondents whether, during the last month, they came across any information they knew or learned was fake news. The paper reports the share of respondents answering yes in each country (36%, 19%, 29%) with explicit sample sizes. This is a self-reported share of respondents who encountered misinformation, which meets the RECALL criterion.

estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report having come across information in the last month that they knew or learned was fake news

estimates.denominator: 745 US respondents completing both waves of an online quota-sampled panel (Lightspeed Kantar), quota-sampled on gender, age, region, income/social class and education against US Census benchmarks

estimates.page_loc: Conclusion, p. 461 (first reported in Results, RQ1a and b, p. 455: 'In the United States, the fraction believing they were exposed is 36 percent')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own judgement, with the survey supplying the definition 'news that was produced in order to give false information'. The authors stress the measure is not a proxy for actual exposure and is vulnerable to false positives correlated with partisanship in the US and to recall error.
estimates.moderator_quote: Belief in Exposure to False News was measured by asking (in the English versions): “During the last month have you come across any information that you know or learned was ‘fake news’ (news that was produced in order to give false information)?”
estimates.notes: One-month recall window. denom_scope is population per the survey rule. breadth is coded fabricated because the question's parenthetical defines fake news by deliberate production of false information. The denominator used is the number completing both waves (745; the same figure appears in the note to Table 3); the logistic regressions run on a smaller listwise n of 685. Not a probability sample: an online quota panel, with weighting efficiency reported (99.1% wave 1, 90.5% wave 2) in place of a response rate.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) 'about a third of pooled respondents across the three countries report that they believe they had been exposed to false news' — a vague pooled restatement of the three country figures already extracted; (2) the verification measure ('Have you further checked the "fake news" to compare it to other sources of information?', with 'roughly half to two-thirds of respondents in each country reporting they attempted verification', and Table 2/Table 3 percentages) — a fact-checking behaviour, not exposure to or sharing of misinformation, so out of scope; (3) the by-vote-choice breakdown in Table 2 (belief in exposure: US 48% among right-wing voters vs 28% among others; UK 16% vs 21%; France 25% vs 30%) — subgroup figures; the paper's headline descriptive result is the three country-level fractions, and the party contrast is developed through the regressions (OR 2.34 for Trump voters), so only the main country figures are extracted; (4) the by-social-media-use breakdown in Table 3 (belief in exposure: US non-users 25%, general users 33%, political users 71%; UK 11/18/60; France 20/30/61) — again subgroups of the same country estimates; (5) the post hoc reasons for suspecting a story is fake (untrue on its face: 56% US, 53% UK, 53% France; and Trump supporters 63%, 21%, 29%) — beliefs about detection cues, not exposure; (6) all figures the paper cites from other studies (Pew's 'about a third of Americans believed they had seen fabricated news', Guess et al.'s 27% visiting a faux-news site, Allcott and Gentzkow's 15% recalling a faux-news headline, the 'about a quarter report having shared such stories') — cited from elsewhere and therefore excluded. Uncertainty: the descriptive percentages are read from the narrative and Figure 1 rather than from a numeric table, and the denominators used (745 / 829 / 1,182 completing both waves) are the panel sizes reported in the Data section and the note to Table 3, which are larger than the listwise regression n's (685 / 733 / 1,137).

rob.design: Two-wave online panel survey around the 2016-2017 national elections in the United States, the United Kingdom and France, fielded by Lightspeed Kantar Group with quota sampling on gender, age, region, income/social class and education against government population data (US Census 2010; UK Labour Force Survey and Census 2011; INSEE). Wave 1: France 5-13 April 2017, UK 2-12 May 2017, US 2-20 May 2017. Wave 2 (carrying the dependent variables): France 16 May - 1 June 2017, UK and US 9-30 June 2017. Completing both waves: US n=745, UK n=829, France n=1,182. No response rate is reported because of the panel design; weighting efficiency was 99.1% (wave 1) and 90.5% (wave 2), against Kantar's recommended 70% minimum. Both dependent variables are dichotomous self-reports; data analysed unweighted with country-specific logistic regressions (listwise n = 685 / 733 / 1,137) plus a pooled model with country dummies. The authors devote a section to design limitations: the measure captures belief about exposure and not actual exposure, is subject to respondent false positives and negatives that are non-randomly distributed (notably partisan false positives in the US), to recall error, and, for the verification item, to possible social desirability bias.
rob.item6_quote: Belief in Exposure to False News was measured by asking (in the English versions): “During the last month have you come across any information that you know or learned was ‘fake news’ (news that was produced in order to give false information)?”
rob.item10_quote: In the United States, the fraction believing they were exposed is 36 percent, which is slightly higher than previous reports using different measures (Barthel et al. 2016; Guess et al. 2018). The figure is smaller for France at 29 percent, and smaller still in the United Kingdom at 19 percent, as Figure 1 shows.
